wstep: This card describes how to dry finely chopped garlic in a dehydrator at 140 °F (60 °C) and grind the dried garlic.

akapity: Peel the garlic cloves and chop them finely; no other pretreatment is needed.
MSU rates garlic as “good” for drying; MSU gives no reason for this rating.
Arrange the prepared vegetables on trays in a single or thin layer, no more than 1/2 inch (about 13 mm) deep.
Dry the vegetables at 140 °F (60 °C) in a dehydrator or oven.
Do not dry vegetables outdoors: dry them under the controlled conditions of an oven or dehydrator.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Only use an oven if it can be set as low as 140 °F (60 °C); if it cannot go that low, the vegetables cook instead of drying.
In an oven, keep 140–150 °F (about 60–66 °C): place a calibrated oven thermometer on the rack or tray and check it every 2 hours throughout drying.
Leave the oven door open 2–3 inches (about 5–7.5 cm) so moisture can escape.
In a conventional oven, drying can take up to twice as long as in a dehydrator, depending on air circulation.
Dry the garlic in a dehydrator for 6–8 hours.
General rule: vegetables are dried until brittle; they then contain about 10% moisture and do not need conditioning.
Grind the dried garlic in a food mill, food processor or blender.
Pack only completely cooled vegetables: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Store the dried vegetables in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Keep the powder in airtight containers: dry foods kept out of airtight containers may absorb moisture from the air, and powders may clump.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried food to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store the dried vegetables in a cool, dry, dark place.
Dried vegetables keep about half as long as dried fruit: according to Clemson HGIC, about 6 months at 60 °F and 3 months at 80 °F.

Do not keep dried garlic in oil at room temperature: oil keeps out oxygen, and spores of Clostridium botulinum may already be present in garlic and herbs; without oxygen, with low acid and at room temperature they can produce a deadly toxin.
Drying does not make this safe: according to UGA, dried garlic and herbs may still not be dry enough to give a safe product.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): if you put dried garlic in oil, keep the oil in the refrigerator and use it within 4 days of making it, or freeze it.
Check the dried vegetables often (glass shows condensation); if they have taken up moisture but are not spoiled, use them at once or dry them again and repack them.
Throw away mouldy dried vegetables; also throw away any that smell off.
